questions.question: In a multistage game with observed actions, player $i$ follows strategy $s_i$. Which modified strategy $\hat s_i$ counts as a one-stage deviation from $s_i$ at the history $h^t$?
options: One that changes the action at $h^t$ and then best responds at later histories
One that changes the actions at $h^t$ and at every other history of stage $t$
One that changes every player's action at $h^t$ and then returns to $s$
One that changes the action at $h^t$ only and agrees with $s_i$ later on

questions.question: When player $i$ tests a one-stage deviation at history $h^t$ of a multistage game, which payoffs does she compare in the subgame starting at $h^t$?
options: Only the stage-$t$ payoffs, since later play is left unchanged
Total continuation payoffs, including how others react later
The stage-$t$ payoff of the deviation against the stage equilibrium payoff
Payoffs from stage $t+1$ on, since stage $t$ is already fixed

questions.question: To show with the one-stage deviation principle that a strategy profile $s$ of a multistage game is subgame perfect, at which histories must one-stage deviations be checked?
options: Only at histories reached when everyone follows $s$
Only at the empty history at the start of the game
At every history, on and off the equilibrium path
Only at histories in which some player has deviated

questions.question: The one-stage deviation principle states that a profile $s$ of a multistage game is subgame perfect if and only if no player has a profitable one-stage deviation at any history. Which direction carries its real content?
options: No profitable one-stage deviation implies subgame perfect
Subgame perfection rules out every profitable one-stage deviation
Both directions are equally immediate from the definitions
Neither, since the result only applies to finite games

questions.question: The one-stage deviation principle is stated for multistage games with observed actions. What does the observed-actions assumption contribute to it?
options: Each history then starts a subgame in which the deviation can be evaluated
It guarantees that every stage game has a Nash equilibrium in pure actions
It makes the infinite sums of discounted stage payoffs converge
It ensures that players never want to deviate from equilibrium play

questions.question: In the prisoner's dilemma with $v(C,C)=(3,3)$, $v(C,D)=(0,5)$, $v(D,C)=(5,0)$, $v(D,D)=(1,1)$, played infinitely often with average payoff $(1-\delta)\sum_{t\ge0}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)$ and $\delta=0.6$, both players play $C$ while every earlier profile was $(C,C)$, and $D$ otherwise. What does player 1 get from playing $D$ once at the start and then following the rule?

In the prisoner's dilemma with $v(C,C)=(3,3)$, $v(C,D)=(0,5)$, $v(D,C)=(5,0)$, $v(D,D)=(1,1)$, played infinitely often with average payoff $(1-\delta)\sum_{t\ge0}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)$ and $\delta=0.7$, both players play $C$ while every earlier profile was $(C,C)$, and $D$ otherwise. After a history with a $D$, what does player 1 get from playing $C$ once and then following the rule?

In the prisoner's dilemma with $v(C,C)=(3,3)$, $v(C,D)=(0,5)$, $v(D,C)=(5,0)$, $v(D,D)=(1,1)$, played infinitely often with average payoff $(1-\delta)\sum_{t\ge0}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)$ and $\delta=0.9$, both players play $C$ at every history. What does player 1 get from playing $D$ once and then following this rule?

In the prisoner's dilemma with $v(C,C)=(3,3)$, $v(C,D)=(0,5)$, $v(D,C)=(5,0)$, $v(D,D)=(1,1)$, played infinitely often with average payoff $(1-\delta)\sum_{t\ge0}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)$, both players play $D$ at every history. For which $\delta\in(0,1)$ does this profile pass every one-stage deviation test?
options: Only for $\delta\ge\tfrac{1}{2}$
Only for $\delta\le\tfrac{1}{2}$
For no $\delta\in(0,1)$
For every $\delta\in(0,1)$

questions.question: The sufficiency proof of the one-stage deviation principle takes a profitable deviation with finitely many changes and as few changes as possible. Why does it look at the last history where this deviation changes behaviour?
options: It is followed only by $s_i$, so it is itself a one-stage deviation
Because the last change always yields the largest stage payoff
Because discounting makes the last change worth the most
Because earlier changes are never reached on the deviation path

questions.question: For an infinite multistage game, the one-stage deviation principle assumes total payoff $\sum_{t\ge0}\delta^{t}v_i^t(a^t)$ with $\delta\in(0,1)$ and bounded stage payoffs. What does this hypothesis secure in the proof?
options: That every stage game has a unique Nash equilibrium
That players observe all past actions before each stage
That some profitable deviation has finitely many changes
That the best deviation always changes only one action

questions.question: In a multistage game with finitely many stages and observed actions, checking every one-stage deviation at every history amounts to which familiar procedure?
options: Checking only that the whole game's strategy profile is a Nash equilibrium
Eliminating strictly dominated actions in each stage game separately
Verifying optimality by backward induction, stage by stage
Checking that a stage Nash equilibrium is played on the path

questions.question: A prisoner's dilemma has $v(C,C)=(3,3)$, $v(C,D)=(0,6)$, $v(D,C)=(6,0)$, $v(D,D)=(1,1)$, played infinitely often with average payoff $(1-\delta)\sum_{t\ge0}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)$. Both players play $C$ while every earlier profile was $(C,C)$, and $D$ otherwise. For which $\delta$ is there no profitable one-stage deviation?
options: $\delta\ge\tfrac{1}{2}$
$\delta\ge\tfrac{3}{5}$
$\delta\ge\tfrac{2}{5}$
$\delta\ge\tfrac{2}{3}$

questions.question: In the prisoner's dilemma with $v(C,C)=(3,3)$, $v(C,D)=(0,5)$, $v(D,C)=(5,0)$, $v(D,D)=(1,1)$, played infinitely often, both players play $C$ while every earlier profile was $(C,C)$, and $D$ otherwise. Player 1 considers $\hat s_1$: play $D$ at the on-path history of stage 3 and at every later history. Let $\tilde s_1$ play $D$ at that history only. Which statement about $\hat s_1$ is correct?
options: It is not a one-stage deviation, yet its path equals that of $\tilde s_1$
It is a one-stage deviation, since its only change of plan is at stage 3
It is not a one-stage deviation, and its path differs from that of $\tilde s_1$
It is a one-stage deviation, since the rule prescribes $D$ later anyway

questions.question: In the prisoner's dilemma with $v(C,C)=(3,3)$, $v(C,D)=(0,5)$, $v(D,C)=(5,0)$, $v(D,D)=(1,1)$, played three times with total payoffs and $\delta=1$, both players play $C$ while every earlier profile was $(C,C)$, and $D$ otherwise. Which one-stage deviation test fails?
options: At the start: $D$ raises player 1's total from $9$ to $11$
At stage 3 after a deviation: $C$ raises her payoff from $1$ to $3$
None: every one-stage deviation lowers player 1's payoff
At stage 3 after $(C,C),(C,C)$: $D$ raises her payoff from $3$ to $5$

questions.question: In an infinitely played stage game with average discounted payoffs, both players play $C$ while every earlier profile was $(C,C)$, and $D$ otherwise, where $(D,D)$ is a Nash equilibrium of the stage game. Why can the one-stage test at histories containing a $D$ never fail?
options: Because such histories are never reached, so play at them is irrelevant
Because the future stays $(D,D)$ regardless, and $D$ is a stage best response
Because the deviator is already being punished and cannot be punished more
Because discounting makes deviations off the equilibrium path worth less

questions.question: In the prisoner's dilemma with $v(C,C)=(3,3)$, $v(C,D)=(0,5)$, $v(D,C)=(5,0)$, $v(D,D)=(1,1)$, played forever with average payoff $(1-\delta)\sum_{t\ge0}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)$, both play $C$ in normal stages; after a normal stage whose profile is not $(C,C)$, one stage of $(D,D)$ follows, then normal play. For which $\delta\in(0,1)$ are all one-stage tests passed?
options: Only $\delta\ge\tfrac{1}{2}$
Only $\delta\ge\tfrac{2}{3}$
Every $\delta\in(0,1)$
No $\delta\in(0,1)$

questions.question: A stage game adds action $P$ to the prisoner's dilemma with $v(C,C)=(3,3)$, $v(C,D)=(0,5)$, $v(D,C)=(5,0)$, $v(D,D)=(1,1)$: $v(D,P)=(1,0)$, $v(P,D)=(0,1)$, other profiles with $P$ give $(0,0)$. Played forever with average payoff $(1-\delta)\sum_{t\ge0}\delta^{t}v_i(a^t)$, both play $C$ while all earlier profiles were $(C,C)$, else $P$. For which $\delta$ is this subgame perfect?
options: $\delta\ge\tfrac{2}{5}$
$\delta\ge\tfrac{1}{2}$
No $\delta\in(0,1)$
Every $\delta\in(0,1)$

questions.question: Player 1 chooses $a$ (stage payoff $0$) or $b$ (stage payoff $1$) in every stage forever, payoffs unaffected by others, and is ranked by the long-run average stage payoff without discounting. Which statement about the strategy "always play $a$" is correct?
options: It passes every one-stage test, yet "always $b$" does strictly better
It fails the one-stage test, since $b$ once raises the long-run average
It is optimal, since it passes every one-stage deviation test
It fails the one-stage test only at the empty history
